task: Horizon 3 of the llm-http-proxy project (horizons 1 and 2 landed the standalone package and the seven correctness review fixes #1-#7; horizon 2 is green at both gate levels). This horizon executes the three deferred code-review findings — #9 (collapse the fake per-provider parser registry to a single defaultParser with a clean-break public surface), #10 (remove dead app.module.ts scaffolding, move install() into a bootstrap hook), #8 (kNoCapture negative capture-decision cache) — plus the user-promoted first slice of the vision-track enforced-order request/response transformer pipeline with Content-Length accounting. Version bumps 0.1.0 -> 0.2.0 to record the #9 clean break. Holding for later horizons: the transformer response strand, latency-budget benchmark (blocked on methodology sign-off), OTEL exporter demo (blocked on peer-dep decision), package publish (blocked on name/version decision).

analysis.objective: Execute llm-http-proxy horizon 3: land the three deferred code-review findings — #9 (collapse the fake per-provider parser registry to a single defaultParser with a clean-break index.ts public surface and in-lockstep consumer update), #10 (remove dead app.module.ts scaffolding, move install() into a bootstrap hook), #8 (kNoCapture negative capture-decision cache) — plus the promoted first slice of the vision-track enforced-order request/response transformer pipeline with Content-Length accounting, all with both gate levels green.
analysis.successDefinition: Done and correct when: (1) provider-parser.ts keeps only defaultParser (plus ProviderParser/ParseResult types and default helpers), PARSERS_BY_HOST/resolveParser/parserToTokenCounter and the five parser aliases are deleted, index.ts no longer exports resolveParser/parseCall, a grep confirms src/app.module.ts is the sole consumer and compiles against the new surface, and package.json + index.ts carry VERSION 0.2.0; (2) src/app.module.ts has no sample*/void import-time lines and calls llmHttpInterceptor.install() from an OnApplicationBootstrap hook; (3) interceptor.ts sets a kNoCapture tag on first shouldCapture=false and writeWrapper/endWrapper/onWrapper short-circuit on it, with a regression test proving shouldCapture no longer re-runs for non-matching requests while matching requests still capture; (4) a request transformer runs before send, the wire Content-Length equals the transformed body's Buffer.byteLength when replacement happened, and tests prove ordering and intact mutated-body delivery; (5) both gate levels are green — package tsc/eslint/jest/build and repo-root nest build + root jest — with the package dist rebuilt first.
assumptions: Horizon 2 is landed and both gate levels are green per state.md (package jest 89/89 + root gates) — taken as given, not revalidated.
parseCall may remain as an internal helper in provider-parser.ts consumed by interceptor.ts; only its public index.ts export is dropped.
src/app.module.ts is the only consumer of resolveParser/parseCall/parser aliases — verified by repo-wide grep during discovery.
The #9 version bump is an in-package version marker (0.1.0 -> 0.2.0) recording the clean break; final package identity and publish verification remain blocked by the open blockers.md decision.
A request's hostname/host header is fixed after ClientRequest construction, so a per-request kNoCapture tag cannot go stale.
The transformer first slice is synchronous with a passthrough default when the option is absent, so existing behavior is unchanged unless a consumer opts in.
Content-Length is rewritten only for captured request bodies actually replaced — chunked/gzip/absent-header requests pass through untouched, byte length computed via Buffer.byteLength.
risks: Stale kNoCapture tag if a request object were reused or its host mutated after construction — the invariant is proven by a regression test, not just assumed.

#9 clean-break blast radius: any consumer of resolveParser/parseCall/parser aliases beyond src/app.module.ts breaks the root build the moment index.ts drops the exports — grep every import first and update the consumer in lockstep before rebuilding the package dist.
#10 startup-window gap: moving install() off import time means traffic before/without the bootstrap hook is silently not intercepted — a behavior change tests must pin down.

Transformer slice vs. the deferred latency bar: transformers do work on the request path, which the blocked benchmark's 'no work beyond body capture' phrase forbids — the promoted slice implicitly rewrites that vision bar.

Content-Length/response-buffer correctness edges: rewriting Content-Length on a mutated body can corrupt chunked/gzip/absent requests if the wrong unit is used, and buffering a full response changes streaming semantics — first-slice tests cover passthrough cases as well as mutated ones.
outOfScope: Transformer response strand (responseTransform buffered path) — deferred to horizon 4 by the size cut; the slice-spec ADR pins its contract.
Latency-budget benchmark — blocked on the benchmark-methodology sign-off in blockers.md.
OTEL span exporter demo — blocked on the optional @opentelemetry/* peer-dependency decision.
Package identity/name decision, publish verification, and actual npm publish — blocked on the open name/version decision; only the in-package 0.2.0 marker is in scope.
Async/streaming/chunk-level and gzip/encoding-aware transformers — beyond the enforced-order + Content-Length first slice.
Streaming/SSE/TLS/retries/auth provider features — decisions.md fixes all extension seams as interface-only.
Optional thin Nest adapter and repo-root workspaces/CI restructure.
Public-API semver freeze for LlmLogEntry/LlmLoggingOptions — the #9 clean break is the only deliberate API change.
analysis.domainShapeReason: Pure machinery engineering — collapsing a parser registry, caching a capture decision, moving a lifecycle hook, inserting transform/Content-Length logic in an HTTP interception pipeline — with no business entities, rules, or workflows; matches the binding domain-shape-fit decision in decisions.md.

ubiquitousLanguage.meaning: The single provider parser replacing the fake per-provider registry (PARSERS_BY_HOST, resolveParser, five aliases); the object the interceptor uses unless a custom providerParser is supplied.
The sole parser extension point in InterceptorOptions; when supplied it fully replaces defaultParser, and no per-provider routing remains.
Dropping resolveParser/parseCall from the public index.ts surface with an in-lockstep consumer update and version bump, rather than deprecated shims.
The negative symbol tag set on a request the first time shouldCapture returns false, short-circuiting re-tests in writeWrapper, endWrapper, and onWrapper.
The OnApplicationBootstrap/onModuleInit lifecycle hook replacing import-time llmHttpInterceptor.install(), paired with the existing onApplicationShutdown restore().
The enforced-order transform seams: request body transformed before send, response body transformed before it returns to the caller.
Rewriting the request Content-Length header to the transformed body's actual byte length so a mutated request body reaches the wire with a correct header.
The mutation-delivery proof bar: a mutated request body reaches the wire and a mutated response body reaches the caller unaltered and in order.

phases.name: defaultParser clean break in the provider parser
phases.goal: Collapse the fake per-provider parser registry to a single defaultParser: export the unexported genericChatParser as defaultParser, delete PARSERS_BY_HOST/resolveParser/parserToTokenCounter and the five identical aliases, stop exporting parseCall publicly (keep it internal for interceptor.ts), drop resolveParser/parseCall from index.ts, re-export defaultParser, bump VERSION 0.1.0->0.2.0 in BOTH index.ts and package.json. Rewrite src/app.module.ts customProviderParser.extractModel to delegate to defaultParser (keeping the unknown->elenwatch-fallback override) and rewrite the two registry-identity tests in provider-parser.test.ts while carrying the behavioral suites over.

phases.goal: Add the kNoCapture symbol tag to interceptor.ts request tagging: the first time shouldCapture returns false for a request, set the tag, and short-circuit onWrapper/writeWrapper/endWrapper before any re-run of shouldCapture (tag in the wrapper call sites, never inside shouldCapture, so the exported bare-{hostname} unit-test semantics stay intact). Add a regression test proving with a non-matching provider that shouldCapture runs exactly once per request, while matching requests still capture.
inputs: interceptor.ts shouldCapture call sites (onWrapper, writeWrapper, endWrapper) + symbol-tag infra (kCapture, wrapper symbols, tag()/Tagged)
Fixed-after-construction hostname invariant (a per-request kNoCapture tag cannot go stale)

phases.expectedResult: kNoCapture cache landed in interceptor.ts: all three wrappers short-circuit on it after the first negative shouldCapture decision, and a new regression test proves shouldCapture no longer re-runs for non-matching requests while matching requests still capture; package jest + both gate levels green with dist rebuilt.

rubric.label: kNoCapture tag lives at the wrapper call sites, not inside shouldCapture
rubric.ruleStatement: The kNoCapture tag is read and set exclusively in interceptor.ts wrapper call sites (onWrapper, writeWrapper, endWrapper); shouldCapture stays a pure decision function with no symbol-tag reads, writes, or dependencies.
passCriteria: No kNoCapture symbol reference (read or write) appears inside the shouldCapture function body in interceptor.ts.
shouldCapture still takes only (req, providers) and computes the hostname match; its body is behaviorally identical to the pre-change version.
The existing exported bare-{hostname} shouldCapture unit test passes unchanged, with plain {hostname} objects and no installed interceptor.
The tag is set via tag(this) in a wrapper immediately after a first shouldCapture false return.
failureExamples: kNoCapture is set or read inside shouldCapture, so calling the exported function with a bare {hostname} object now touches tag infrastructure.
shouldCapture gains an import or closure dependency on tag()/Tagged, breaking direct unit-test use.
The cache write happens after the wrapper already returned, so the same wrapper re-runs shouldCapture on its next invocation.

rubric.label: onWrapper, writeWrapper, and endWrapper all short-circuit on kNoCapture
rubric.ruleStatement: Once a negative capture decision is cached on a request, all three wrapper call sites skip shouldCapture entirely — the cache guard is checked before the decision, not after or only in one wrapper.
passCriteria: onWrapper's decision branch is guarded by a kNoCapture check preceding its shouldCapture call.
writeWrapper's decision branch is guarded by a kNoCapture check preceding its shouldCapture call.
endWrapper's decision branch is guarded by a kNoCapture check preceding its shouldCapture call.
Each guard short-circuits with the same observable behavior as the would-be false decision (no attachCapture, no appendChunk, original write/end still forwarded).
failureExamples: writeWrapper caches the negative but endWrapper still invokes shouldCapture on its first end() call.
onWrapper (error-listener attach) ignores the cached negative and calls shouldCapture again.
A guard is placed after shouldCapture runs, so it prevents nothing.

rubric.label: Capture decisions are unchanged for matching and non-matching requests
rubric.ruleStatement: The cache is pure memoization: every request that captured before still captures, every request that did not still does not, regardless of which wrapper entry path the request exercises first.
passCriteria: A matching-provider request still produces exactly one log entry with the same request/response body content as before (existing capture tests pass unmodified).
A non-matching-provider request still produces zero entries across any wrapper ordering.
A request entering only through end(body) with a non-matching host yields the same no-capture outcome as one entering through write.
Consecutive decision paths on the same request agree: the first (cache-populating) call and every later short-circuited path return the same capture decision.
failureExamples: A false positive: a non-matching request produces an entry because a wrapper path not covered by the cache re-evaluates and mis-decides.
A false negative: a matching request emits nothing because a stale or prototype-scoped negative tag suppresses capture.
The cache changes payload behavior: a tagged request skips appendChunk or reflected write/end forwarding that it previously performed.

rubric.label: Regression test proves shouldCapture runs exactly once for a non-matching request
rubric.ruleStatement: A new test instruments call frequency and demonstrates that for a non-matching provider, shouldCapture executes exactly once across the full write/end/error lifecycle, while a matching request still captures.
passCriteria: A new test spies on or counts calls to shouldCapture and asserts count === 1 for a non-matching provider across write + end (+ error) on a real patched wrapper path.
The same test asserts the single call returned false (the one call is the cache miss).
The same or paired test asserts a matching-provider request still produces a capture entry.
The test goes red when run against the pre-change interceptor source (the decision runs 2+ times).
failureExamples: The test counts calls on a mocked function but never drives the real patched ClientRequest.prototype paths.
The test only exercises the write path and misses a re-run in end or on('error').
The test asserts entry production but not the call count.

rubric.label: Cache is per-request, repeatable, and rollback-clean
rubric.ruleStatement: The kNoCapture tag is scoped to the individual ClientRequest instance — never on the prototype, module-level state, or any shared object — so it cannot go stale, survives repeated install/restore cycles, and leaves nothing behind after restore().
passCriteria: kNoCapture is only written via tag(this)/tag(req) on the request instance; no occurrence sets it on ClientRequest.prototype or a module-level Map/WeakMap.
Repeated install -> request -> restore cycles produce identical capture decisions with no carry-over of cached negatives between cycles.
A second Interceptor installed while the first is active neither adds nor skips shouldCapture calls beyond the cache intent.
restore() reinstates original write/end by reference identity with no tag-related cleanup required.
failureExamples: kNoCapture is set on ClientRequest.prototype, so the first non-matching request permanently negative-caches every later request.
A module-level cache holds tagged request objects and leaks them after restore().
The wrapper reads a cached negative before reflecting the original write/end, altering request behavior instead of only the capture decision.

phases.healerHint: Most likely the guard lands only in writeWrapper or inside shouldCapture itself, so end/on re-run the decision and the exactly-once test fails — move the kNoCapture read and set into all three wrapper call sites, keep shouldCapture pure, and re-run the counting test plus the bare-{hostname} shouldCapture unit test.

phases.name: body transformation: first-slice contract ADR
phases.goal: Author the transformer first-slice slice spec: commit the exact transformer signatures, InterceptorOptions field names (requestTransform?/responseTransform? or decided equivalents), enforced ordering (request transform before send, response transform before caller sees the body), the Content-Length rewrite policy (rewrite only captured request bodies actually replaced, Buffer.byteLength utf8, chunked/gzip/absent pass through), and the response buffering boundary (buffer+transform only captured non-streaming responses; async/streaming/chunk-level and encoding-aware transformation stays out of scope). Log the vision-track promotion decision in decisions.md.
inputs: stage2 required material: Transformer first-slice API contract + success-definition wording from analysis
docs/roadmaps/llm-http-proxy/ decisions.md for the promotion log + roadmap dir for the spec
phases.expectedResult: One slice-spec ADR under docs/roadmaps/llm-http-proxy/ that pins the transformer signatures, InterceptorOptions field names, ordering guarantee, Content-Length policy, and response-buffering boundary, with the scope promotion logged as a decisions.md line.

rubric.label: InterceptorOptions field names pinned to one decision
rubric.ruleStatement: The ADR resolves the option naming to exactly one concrete field per transform — requestTransform? / responseTransform? or a decided equivalent — used consistently throughout, with no alternatives, placeholders, or 'decide later' wording left in the document.
passCriteria: A grep of the ADR body finds exactly one resolved InterceptorOptions field name for the request transform and exactly one for the response transform, and the same names appear in every signature and usage example in the document.
The literal phrase 'or decided equivalents' (or 'TBD' / 'decide later' / 'undecided') appears nowhere in the ADR body.
Each pinned option field's declared type points at the exact transformer type from the signatures section, not a generic function type.
failureExamples: The ADR still reads 'requestTransform?/responseTransform? or decided equivalents', so an executor cannot edit options.ts without inventing the contract.
One section uses requestTransform while another uses transformRequest, leaving two candidate names in the same document.
The field names are pinned but their type is written as 'a transform function' with no reference to the pinned signatures.

rubric.label: Transformer signatures fully specified and internally consistent
rubric.ruleStatement: The ADR pins callable TypeScript signatures — parameter list, parameter types, return type, sync-or-async, and the meaning of an undefined/void return — so an implementer can write the interface with zero invention.
passCriteria: The ADR contains a TypeScript interface block for both transform functions with every parameter and the return type written out explicitly.
It states in prose whether the transform may be async (Promise-returning) or must be sync, and what an undefined/void return means (pass-through, keep the original body).
The signature's units reconcile with the Content-Length section: the transform's output type is the thing Buffer.byteLength(..., 'utf8') is computed over.
failureExamples: The signature is written as '(body) => body' with types and semantics left to the implementer.
The prose allows async transforms but the interface block has no Promise return type and no rule for a rejected transform.
The signature takes and returns a string while the Content-Length policy computes byte length on the output — the two sections contradict each other.

rubric.label: Enforced ordering anchored to concrete seams
rubric.ruleStatement: The ADR pins the ordering guarantee as exact seams: the request transform runs before the request bytes forward to the pristine original (wire), and the response transform runs before the caller sees the body, with the emission-path relationship resolved and throw behavior specified.
passCriteria: The request seam is anchored to a named point in the write/end wrapper flow (before forwarding to the original) so writeWrapper and endWrapper cannot disagree.
The response seam names both relationships: before the body reaches the caller AND whether emitLogEntry's JSON.parse sees the pre- or post-transform body.
The ADR states what happens when a transform throws, on the request strand and on the response strand (abort/replace vs catch-and-pass-through).
failureExamples: The ADR says 'request transformed before send' but never anchors send to a wrapper seam.
Response ordering is given only against the caller while the pre/post-transform body for parseCall/redaction is left unspecified.
Transform-throws behavior is absent, forcing the executor to guess between aborting and passing through.

rubric.label: Content-Length policy has a verdict for every header state
rubric.ruleStatement: The Content-Length rewrite policy is exhaustive: rewrite only when a captured request body was actually replaced by the transform, recompute as Buffer.byteLength of the transformed bytes as utf8, and pass through for every other state (not captured, body unchanged, header absent, chunked, gzip).
passCriteria: The ADR rows through each header state with an explicit rewrite-or-pass-through verdict: Content-Length absent, Content-Length present with a replaced body, transfer-encoding chunked, and content-encoding gzip.

The rewrite rule states the length is recomputed as Buffer.byteLength(transformedBody, 'utf8') and applied only when the captured body was actually replaced (no-op transforms keep the original header).
The ADR confirms the default behavior — no transform configured — leaves the header untouched, preserving today's passthrough.
failureExamples: The ADR says 'update the Content-Length header' without mentioning chunked, gzip, or absent-header cases.
The policy rewrites Content-Length even when the transform returned the body unchanged.
Length is specified via string .length rather than byte length, under-counting multi-byte UTF-8 payloads.

rubric.label: Response buffering boundary explicit and out-of-scope seams named
rubric.ruleStatement: The ADR states the buffering-and-transform boundary in terms of exactly which responses qualify (captured, non-streaming), and names each out-of-scope seam (async, streaming/chunk-level, encoding-aware) explicitly so the next horizon cannot silently extend the slice.
passCriteria: The ADR states exactly which responses get buffered+transformed (captured, non-streaming) and defines 'non-streaming' concretely (full-buffer capture already in place, no SSE/streaming).
Each out-of-scope seam appears by name in an explicit out-of-scope list: async, streaming/chunk-level, encoding-aware transformation.
The ADR ties the boundary to the existing capture machinery so the slice only covers responses that are already fully buffered today.
failureExamples: The ADR describes buffering 'responses' without carving out streaming.
Encoding-aware transformation is never mentioned, leaving gzip/chunked decode ambiguity.
The out-of-scope list omits chunk-level transform, and a later phase cites this ADR as authorizing per-chunk mutation.

rubric.label: Promotion logged in decisions.md and ADR file present and unique
rubric.ruleStatement: The vision-track promotion decision is recorded in decisions.md as a dated line naming the ADR file and the promotion verdict, and exactly one slice-spec ADR file exists under the roadmap directory, so horizon-4 can locate the binding contract.
passCriteria: docs/roadmaps/llm-http-proxy/decisions.md contains a new dated line recording that the transformer first slice is promoted from vision-deferred to an ADR-bound contract.
The decisions.md promotion line names the ADR file path under docs/roadmaps/llm-http-proxy/.
Exactly one slice-spec ADR markdown file exists in that directory and it contains the option-names, signatures, ordering, Content-Length, and buffering-boundary sections this rubric checks.
failureExamples: No new decisions.md line exists, so horizon-4 cannot tell the slice became a binding contract.
The ADR file exists but decisions.md never names it.
Two near-identical spec files (draft + final) exist, leaving ambiguity about which is the contract.

phases.healerHint: The ADR most likely reads complete but still contains a placeholder (the phase goal literally says 'requestTransform?/responseTransform? or decided equivalents') and a Content-Length policy with no chunked/gzip/absent verdicts — so grep the draft for 'or decided equivalents' and 'TBD', then pin both option names in one pass and add the Content-Length decision table before grading.

phases.name: body transformation: request strand with Content-Length accounting
phases.goal: Wire the request transformer per the slice-spec signatures into interceptor.ts writeWrapper/endWrapper: between chunk capture and reflectCall, mutate the captured request args so the transformed body hits the wire, then rewrite Content-Length to Buffer.byteLength(utf8) of the transformed body only when a captured body was actually replaced (chunked/gzip/absent-header requests pass through untouched). Absent option = synchronous passthrough so existing behavior is unchanged.
inputs: transformer first-slice ADR (signatures, option names, ordering, Content-Length policy)
phases.expectedResult: Request strand landed: a mutated request body reaches the wire intact and in order with Content-Length equal to its Buffer.byteLength, passthrough cases unchanged, and package jest + both gate levels green with dist rebuilt.
phases.compensation: Delete the additive InterceptorOptions transform fields and the writeWrapper/endWrapper hook — nothing else consumes them in this slice, and the passthrough default restores prior behavior.

rubric.label: Transformed body reaches the wire intact and in order
rubric.ruleStatement: A mutated request body reaches the wire byte-identical to the transformer output and in the original write order.
passCriteria: An on-wire server test (withEntries/post harness) asserts the concatenated received request body equals Buffer.from(transformedBody, 'utf8') byte-for-byte for a transformer that changes body length.
A split-body case (write() + end(chunk)) delivers the transformed body as one coherent sequence on the wire with no original bytes interleaved or duplicated.
The transformed body is written exactly once per request — no echo of the pre-transform body.
Assertions compare Buffers, not strings, so multi-byte/binary transformed output is verified exactly.
failureExamples: Server receives the original body, or a mix of original and transformed bytes.
Transformed bytes arrive reordered or written twice.
Tests assert string equality only, masking byte-level corruption of the wire payload.

rubric.label: Content-Length is byte-accurate and replacement-gated
rubric.ruleStatement: When a captured request body is actually replaced, the request's Content-Length on the wire equals Buffer.byteLength(transformedBody, 'utf8'); otherwise the header is untouched.
passCriteria: Wire-level test confirms the received Content-Length header equals Buffer.byteLength(transformedBody, 'utf8') when replacement happened.
Multi-byte characters are counted as bytes, not characters: a transform that changes the count shifts the header by the byte delta.
Split-body replacement (write() + end(chunk)) yields one Content-Length equal to the total transformed byte length, never per-chunk lengths.
A transformer returning the byte-identical body triggers no header rewrite — the wire header is the caller's original value.
failureExamples: Header carries a stale length computed from the original body.
Header counts UTF-16 characters instead of UTF-8 bytes for multi-byte content.
Split write/end replacement leaves two Content-Length headers or per-chunk lengths.

rubric.label: Passthrough cases are untouched
rubric.ruleStatement: All declared passthrough cases are untouched: with no requestTransformer option the request flows through synchronously with unchanged wire bytes, and chunked/gzip/absent-Content-Length requests never get a Content-Length written or rewritten.
passCriteria: With no requestTransformer option, an on-wire test proves the received body equals the sent body and the Content-Length is the caller's own.
A chunked request (transfer-encoding present, no Content-Length) with a transformer supplied still reaches the wire with chunked framing and no Content-Length added.
Requests with content-encoding gzip or an absent Content-Length header receive no Content-Length write or rewrite from the interceptor.
The pre-existing interceptor suite (singleton guard, off-request-path ordering, finding #4 forwarding, multibyte round-trip) passes unmodified.
failureExamples: Absent-option requests arrive with mutated bytes or a rewritten header.
Chunked or gzip requests gain a Content-Length header, breaking frame/encoding integrity.
Existing tests had to be edited to accommodate the new default path.

rubric.label: Forwarding preserves the write/end argument contract
rubric.ruleStatement: The body replacement preserves the intercepted write/end argument contract — Node's runtime dispatch still receives a coherent (chunk, encoding, callback) list and the stream-return contract is unchanged.
passCriteria: A finding-#4-style test with a length-changing transformer asserts the encoding and callback args are forwarded to the original write/end alongside the replaced chunk.
write() still returns the boolean stream contract and end() still returns the ClientRequest under transformation.
A Buffer replacement coexisting with an encoding argument round-trips without corrupting the request.
failureExamples: Replacement drops the encoding or callback positional arg, corrupting Node's overload dispatch.
write/end return values change when a transformer is present.
The replacement is coerced to a string, silently mis-encoding a Buffer chunk.

rubric.label: Transform once, repeatable, cleanly reversible
rubric.ruleStatement: The request strand is idempotent, repeatable, and reversible: the transformer runs exactly once per request body, repeated identical requests produce identical wire bytes, and removing the additive hooks restores prior behavior.
passCriteria: A counting transformer spy proves exactly one invocation per request body — not once per chunk, not once per write() and again per end().
Two identical requests through the same interceptor instance produce byte-identical wire bodies (deterministic, no hidden state).
install()/restore() cycles with a transformer configured leave no residue: a follow-up request is not double-transformed.
Removing the additive InterceptorOptions transform fields and the write/end hook (the phase's compensation) leaves the pre-slice suite green.
failureExamples: The transformer fires on both write() and end(), doubling the wire body.
A second request through the same instance transforms an already-transformed body.
Stashing the new code leaves pre-slice tests failing or flaky.

rubric.label: Both gate levels green with dist rebuilt
rubric.ruleStatement: The landed slice ships with package jest/lint/build and the root Nest gate green, and dist is rebuilt from the new source so the transform surface is in the shipped artifacts.
passCriteria: npm test and npm run lint pass in packages/llm-http-proxy with the new transform tests included.
npm run build rebuilds dist (tsc cjs+esm + postbuild) and the rebuilt type declarations expose the additive transform fields.
The root Nest level (nest build + jest) is green, run against the freshly rebuilt package dist.
failureExamples: dist is preserved from a pre-slice build, so the shipped .d.ts lacks the transform fields.
The root gate fails or the package gate is skipped while the slice code claims to have landed.
Type-only usage of the transform option passes jest but fails tsc typecheck.

phases.healerHint: The most likely failure is transforming per chunk instead of once over the concatenated capture — a multi-byte character split across write/end gets corrupted and Content-Length goes stale — so accumulate the captured chunks, run the transformer exactly once on the full concatenation at the terminal write/end, and set Content-Length from the resulting Buffer.byteLength.

successCriteria: Findings #9, #10 and #8 are resolved (one phase each except #10 pairs with #9's consumer lockstep), plus the promoted transformer request strand, each with both gate levels green and the package dist rebuilt before root gates; deferred: the transformer response strand, latency benchmark, OTEL exporter, package publish.

parser-seam-default-parser-clean-break: the fake registry (PARSERS_BY_HOST/resolveParser/parserToTokenCounter + 5 aliases) is deleted, index.ts ships the clean-break surface (defaultParser in, resolveParser/parseCall out), app.module.ts compiles in lockstep as the sole consumer, VERSION is 0.2.0 in index.ts AND package.json, registry-identity tests rewritten, behavioral suites green, both gate levels green.

app-module-scaffold-removal-and-bootstrap-lifecycle: sample*/void lines and the redact import are gone, install() fires only from OnApplicationBootstrap (paired with onApplicationShutdown restore()), no import-time patch, both gate levels green.

k-nocapture-capture-decision-cache: kNoCapture tag set on first shouldCapture=false and short-circuits all three wrapper call sites (tag in wrappers, shouldCapture stays pure), a regression test proves shouldCapture runs exactly once for non-matching requests while matching requests still capture, decision parity preserved, both gate levels green.

transformer-slice-spec-adr: one slice-spec ADR pins the transformer signatures, InterceptorOptions field names, enforced ordering, Content-Length rewrite policy (Buffer.byteLength utf8, replacement-gated, chunked/gzip/absent pass through), and response buffering boundary; promotion logged in decisions.md.

request-transform-and-content-length: a mutated request body reaches the wire intact and in order with Content-Length equal to its Buffer.byteLength, transform fn runs once per request body, passthrough (no option / chunked / gzip / absent header) untouched, arg-forwarding contract preserved, both gate levels green with dist rebuilt.
deferred: response-transform-buffered — held for the next Planning Horizon to keep this one small and reviewable; the Planning Brief and project memory carry the context forward (the transformer-slice ADR written this horizon pins the response strand contract).
#8/#9/#10 are in this horizon; the transformer response strand (apply responseTransform before the caller, buffer captured non-streaming responses) is held for horizon 4.

Latency-budget benchmark — a still-binding vision.md success bar; blocked on benchmark-methodology sign-off in blockers.md, and the transformer slice implicitly rewrites the 'no work beyond body capture' bar.
OTEL span exporter demo — a still-binding vision.md success bar; blocked on the optional @opentelemetry/* peer-dependency decision.
Package identity / name decision, publish verification, and npm publish — blocked on the open name/version decision in blockers.md; only the in-package 0.2.0 version marker is in scope here.
Async/streaming/chunk-level and gzip/encoding-aware transformers — explicitly out of the transformer first-slice boundary; passthrough default preserves current behavior.
Streaming/SSE/TLS/retries/auth provider features — decisions.md fixes all extension seams as interface-only, never built-in.
Optional thin Nest adapter and repo-root workspaces/CI restructure — the package stays isolated under packages/ consumed via link: dist.
